title: To Jerusalem: Warnings, a Vow, and a Riot in the Temple
summary: Sailing to Tyre and then traveling to Caesarea, Paul is warned repeatedly, including by the prophet Agabus, that bonds await him in Jerusalem, but he declares himself ready to die for the name of the Lord Jesus. In Jerusalem, James and the elders ask him to join four men completing a vow in the temple to show that he has not taught Jews to abandon the law. Near the end of the week, Jews from Asia accuse him of bringing a Gentile into the temple, a mob seizes him, and Roman soldiers rescue and arrest him.
story: Since 19:21 Paul has been moving toward Jerusalem, and this chapter brings him there. It also closes Paul's career as a free missionary. From this point to the end of Acts he is a prisoner, and the book becomes a series of defenses before crowds, councils, governors, and a king. The arrest echoes Jesus's own last visit to Jerusalem: like his Lord, Paul sets his face toward the city despite warnings, is handed over by his own people to the Gentiles, and hears a crowd shout Away with him. The chapter also shows the Jerusalem church at its most complex, rejoicing in the Gentile mission but anxious about its standing among thousands of Jewish believers zealous for the law.
historical:
Paul arrived in Jerusalem around AD 57, when Antonius Felix was the Roman governor of Judea. The years under Felix were marked by rising unrest: bandits, messianic pretenders, and the Sicarii, the Assassins (from sica, a curved dagger), who killed opponents, including collaborators with Rome, by stabbing them in festival crowds. The commander's question about the Egyptian refers to a real figure. Josephus describes an Egyptian prophet who, under Felix, gathered followers on the Mount of Olives, promising that Jerusalem's walls would fall at his command; Roman troops attacked, and the Egyptian escaped. Josephus gives a much larger number of followers in one of his accounts than Luke's four thousand, and his figures are often inflated.

The Roman commander, a tribune later named as Claudius Lysias (23:26), commanded the cohort garrisoned in the Antonia Fortress, which overlooked the temple courts at their northwest corner and was connected to them by stairs. From there soldiers could reach the courts quickly during festivals. The temple's inner courts were closed to Gentiles by a low barrier with warning notices in Greek and Latin. Two of these Greek inscriptions have been found, and they warn that any foreigner who passes the barrier will have himself to blame for the death that follows. This is the offense Paul was falsely accused of assisting.
cultural:
Paul's friends at Tyre, Caesarea, and elsewhere are family households: wives and children kneel on the beach to pray. Philip, one of the Seven chosen in chapter 6, now lives in Caesarea, and his four unmarried daughters prophesy, fulfilling Joel's promise quoted at Pentecost that sons and daughters would prophesy. Agabus acts out his prophecy with Paul's belt, in the tradition of the Old Testament prophets, who often performed symbolic actions (Jeremiah 13; Ezekiel 4).

The four men of verse 23 are completing a vow, most likely a Nazirite vow (Numbers 6), which ended with shaving the head and offering sacrifices at the temple. Paying the expenses of poorer Nazirites was a recognized act of piety. Paul, returning from Gentile lands, also needed to undergo purification before entering the temple. James's proposal was meant to answer the rumor that Paul taught Jews to forsake Moses, which misrepresented his position; Paul's letters oppose requiring the law of Gentiles and deny that it justifies anyone, but he never told Jewish believers not to circumcise their children. The language Paul uses to address the crowd (verse 40) is called Hebrew, which in this period often meant Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in Judea.
literary: The chapter moves in two halves: the approach to Jerusalem (verses 1-16) and the events in the city (verses 17-40). The first half is built on repeated warnings, each more vivid than the last, climaxing in Agabus's acted prophecy and Paul's reply, and ending with the believers' resigned words, The Lord's will be done, which echo Jesus's prayer in Gethsemane. The second half turns quickly from a hopeful meeting to a violent scene. Luke uses irony in the commander's mistaken identifications: the man he takes for a notorious rebel is a citizen of Tarsus who speaks educated Greek. The chapter ends at a moment of suspense, with a great hush over the crowd as Paul begins to speak.

outline.t: James's counsel and the temple vow

doctrines.note: Paul says he is ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus. The chapter shows that the will of God can lead into suffering rather than away from it.

James and the elders rejoice at what God has done among the Gentiles while seeking to keep faith with Jewish believers zealous for the law. The chapter shows a church holding together two kinds of believers at real cost.

Paul joins in a temple vow and purification to show that he lives in obedience to the law. For Paul, keeping the law as a Jew was a matter of freedom and love for his people, not a way of earning salvation.

words.note: Zelotes, zealous one or zealot. It can describe any person passionately devoted to something, and here it describes thousands of Jewish believers zealous for the law. Paul uses the word of himself before his conversion (Galatians 1:14). Zeal can serve God or blind a person to him.

Apostasia, rebellion or abandonment, the source of the English apostasy. The rumor was that Paul taught Jews apostasy from Moses. The accusation shows how seriously his fellow Jews took the question of faithfulness to the law.

Sikarios, dagger-man or assassin, a Latin word borrowed into Greek and found only here in the New Testament. It names a real group of violent insurgents in Felix's time. The commander's mistake shows how volatile Jerusalem had become.

christ: Luke's telling deliberately recalls the last days of Jesus. Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), predicted he would be handed over to the Gentiles (Luke 18:32), and was met by a crowd crying for his death. Paul follows the same road: a prophet foretells that he will be bound and handed over to the Gentiles, his friends plead with him, and he goes anyway, for the name of the Lord Jesus. The crowd's shout, Away with him, echoes the cry against Jesus (Luke 23:18). Paul is not a second savior, but the pattern shows what it means that disciples follow a crucified Lord: the way of Christ runs through Jerusalem and its suffering, not around it.

hard.q: If the Spirit told believers to warn Paul not to go to Jerusalem, was Paul disobeying the Spirit when he went?
hard.a:
Verse 4 says that through the Spirit the disciples at Tyre kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem, yet in 20:22 Paul says he is going compelled by the Spirit. Read side by side, the Spirit seems to be saying two opposite things.

Most interpreters resolve it this way: the Spirit revealed to the believers what awaited Paul (bonds and suffering, as Agabus's prophecy makes explicit), and they, out of love, drew the conclusion that he should not go. The revelation was the Spirit's; the advice was their own inference from it. Paul accepted the revelation but not the inference, because he believed the Spirit was calling him into that suffering. Agabus himself only predicts what will happen and does not forbid the trip. A minority of interpreters think Paul was in fact mistaken and that the trip was ill-advised, citing the outcome and the questionable wisdom of the vow. Luke's own presentation, however, supports Paul: the believers finally say, The Lord's will be done, and the risen Jesus later tells Paul he must testify in Rome as he has in Jerusalem (23:11).

questions: Paul's friends loved him and wanted to protect him from suffering. How can love sometimes stand in the way of what God is calling someone to do?
James asked Paul to go out of his way to reassure Jewish believers. When is it right to set aside your own freedom to keep peace with other believers?
Rumors about Paul spread and nearly got him killed. How do misunderstandings about people spread in churches, and how can they be stopped?
